hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: pbeesly on scranton ran a credential/secret-collection toolkit (Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-Exfil, Invoke-SeaDukeStage) around the LSASS access.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell (pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) on scranton at 03:05:16, corroborating the anchored LSASS access.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: lsass.exe created C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG and opened the SAM hive with KEY_ALL_ACCESS (0xf003f) on scranton at 03:19, consistent with SAM credential dumping.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No NTDS.dit access, vssadmin/diskshadow/ntdsutil activity found in any dataset.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No LSA Secrets / SECURITY Policy Secrets access or lsadump activity found.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes were normal LSASS cached-credential updates, not dumping.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No DCSync / drsuapi / lsadump replication activity found in any dataset.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: No network sniffing activity found. The only packet-capture behavior is the legitimate Azure Network Watcher agent running 'netsh trace start capture=yes' on scranton.dmevals.local (parent NetworkWatcherAgent.exe from the WindowsAzure GuestAgent). No tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap executables, no pcap/npcap/winpcap/ndiscap driver loads (sysmon event 6), and no pcap/sniff/promiscuous strings in PowerShell script blocks. The PsExec-delivered python.exe on nashua is lateral movement/C2, not sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: PowerShell (pbeesly) and wsmprovhost.exe requested full-access handles (0x1f3fff/0x1fffff) to lsass.exe on scranton and nashua, indicating credential capture from LSASS memory.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogger APIs (GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx) or keylog strings in command lines or script blocks; those checks returned zero hits.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No credential-prompt/GUI input-capture indicators (Get-Credential, Read-Host, CredentialManager) found; checks returned zero hits.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No web-root file writes, IIS/w3wp activity, or login/portal HTTP requests; checks returned zero hits and zeek does not overlap in time.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell script block on scranton reflectively resolves GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle via UnsafeNativeMethods, builds a 'ReflectedDelegate' dynamic assembly and executes base64 shellcode in memory - native API hooking/interception pattern.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed logons and no authentication-failure/lockout messages across all Windows datasets; only successful 4648/4776 logons.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons and no password-referencing process command lines; only unrelated system messages matched 'password'/'failed'.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No SAM/SECURITY hive reads, no hash/crack command lines; LSASS access is benign svchost 0x1000 queries and the only passwordsDB file is a Sysinternals accesschk artifact.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No failed logons to form a spray pattern; 4648 events are PsExec and normal system logons, no user-list tooling.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons or credential-stuffing indicators; only a Credential Guard config line and a legitimate RDP session logon.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card/token interception artifacts were found. 4648 explicit-credential logons reflect credential use by PSEXESVC.exe/svchost.exe (lateral movement), not interception. Credential-named registry writes are benign Windows components (CredentialGuard config by lsass.exe, CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc by services.exe, ContentManagementSDK DeviceTokens by backgroundTaskHost.exe). No smartcard/MFA/token command lines or credential-provider tampering observed.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) coerced its credentials to an attacker-controlled WebDAV/SMB listener at 192.168.0.4: SMB connections to tcp/445 and tcp/139 followed by 36 WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND requests using Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 and DavClnt user agents, with an AUTHORIZATION header and 401->207 responses, enumerating /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z and /webdav/python.exe. Classic T1187 forced-authentication chain.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: Obfuscated PowerShell reflective shellcode loader (UnsafeNativeMethods GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle + DefineDynamicAssembly ReflectedDelegate + base64 PE blob) executed as user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local, corroborated by full-access (0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF) LSASS handles from PowerShell.exe and wsmprovhost.exe on scranton/nashua — consistent with exploitation-driven credential access.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: All cookie-related hits are benign Windows behaviour: DavSetCookie via rundll32/davclnt.dll is the WebDAV redirector storing a WebDAV auth cookie (not a browser session cookie), and the INetCookies file creation is a LocalService svchost writing its own package cookie store. No browser cookie database was read, no cookie-stealer tooling or cookie-bearing HTTP requests were observed. The PsExec/WebDAV python.exe activity is lateral-movement tooling unrelated to cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Multiple unsecured-credential artifacts: hardcoded passwords in scripts ('saribas', 'lolol', 'MyCozyPassw0rd!'), pspasswd staging, and password-protected archive staging.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: pspasswd.exe/pspasswd64.exe staged in Downloads; Rar.exe created password-protected working.zip then sdelete64 wiped it; Invoke-Exfil compressed Downloads with password 'lolol' and exfiltrated using hardcoded creds.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All Password/Credential registry SetValue events are written by legitimate Windows components (svchost IdentityCRL, lsass CredentialGuard, services CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc, winlogon PasswordExpiryNotification).

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No consolehost_history or shell-history access was found in sysmon/security telemetry.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files protected by hardcoded password 'saribas' (coyn5igj.3io.pfx written to Downloads).

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: GptTmpl.inf/SecEdit file writes are performed by svchost.exe (Group Policy client) as normal GPO processing; no Groups.xml/cpassword access observed.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: LSASS full-access handle acquisition by attacker PowerShell/wsmprovhost is consistent with credential-store harvesting, but no explicit vault read was captured.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: Certificate/private-key export to .pfx via PowerShell is consistent with browser/credential-store harvesting, though no explicit browser credential store access was observed.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: Full-access LSASS handles by attacker processes on scranton/nashua are consistent with Credential Manager/DPAPI vault harvesting, but no vault file access was directly observed.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass/.kdbx references in process, file, PowerShell or other-channel data.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: LSASS was opened with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) by a hidden steganographic PowerShell loader (monkey.png -> IEX) on scranton.dmevals.local as pbeesly, indicating credential theft from LSASS memory. This is credential access rather than modification of the authentication process, so the T1556 family itself is not confirmed.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: Type-3 logons are machine-account (NEWYORK$) authentications and 4648 events are pbeesly's own credentials used by PSEXESVC for lateral movement; no DC authentication-process backdoor.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password filter DLL registration, no Notification Packages registry change, no related process/script activity.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 policy changes and no Reversible/Set-ADUser/dsmod activity.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136 events and no MFA-related process or script activity.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 events and no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD hybrid-identity activity.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider/Credential registry changes and no related script activity.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: Network capture/ARP enumeration on scranton is Azure Guest Agent telemetry (netsh trace, ipconfig /all, arp /a spawned by WaAppAgent/GuestAgent/TelemetryService); no AiTM tooling found.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: DNS queries are normal AD/Windows lookups; SMB connections all RSTO to the DC 10.0.0.4 with krb,smb,gssapi; 4697 installs are default Windows services and PSEXESVC. No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Responder MAC 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic placeholder in the lab capture; arp.exe /a is Azure agent telemetry. No gratuitous-ARP or duplicate MAC-to-IP mapping.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP events in any dataset (no 1341/1342/1020/1063, no Zeek dhcp log, no port 67/68 traffic); DHCP spoofing cannot be assessed from this data.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS); the same process was launched by pbeesly with a hidden-window steganographic loader decoding monkey.png and piping to IEX — credential theft from LSASS.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: Three 4769 requests for the krbtgt service with RC4 (0x12) and TicketOptions 0x60810010 by pbeesly and SCRANTON$; unusual but no forged-ticket artifact directly confirmed.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: All observed 4769 service-ticket requests were KDC-issued with Failure Code 0x0; no forged service ticket used without a corresponding KDC request.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: 28 TGS (4769) requests all with RC4 encryption 0x12 targeting machine/service accounts NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$ — RC4 downgrade consistent with Kerberoasting.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: No AS-REP roasting indicators: PowerShell searches for AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth returned zero hits and no pre-auth-disabled 4768 requests were seen.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential activity: LSASS access events with high masks came from legitimate PowerShell.exe (0x1FFFFF) and wsmprovhost.exe (0x1F3FFF) on scranton/nashua, other high-mask accesses were svchost/wininit/csrss, logon process names were Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp, and WMI 5857/5858 events were routine RSOP_ExtensionStatus DeleteInstance by SYSTEM.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie-path file event is a ServiceProfiles\LocalService INetCookies container created by svchost.exe on scranton; no PowerShell cookie/Set-Cookie/session script content and no cookie-bearing web auth in Zeek HTTP (WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND only).

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML/ADFS/token artifacts in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, process command lines, or Zeek HTTP URLs; the only notable PowerShell event is an unrelated in-memory loader script block on scranton with no SAML/token forging content.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No multi-factor authentication request generation activity found. The only T1621 check hit (C355, WMI 5857/5858/5860 in windows.other) is benign Group Policy/RSOP WMI provider activity by SYSTEM/NETWORK SERVICE. Searches for MFA/authenticator/2FA/push in PowerShell script blocks returned 0 rows, no 4625/4771 failed logons exist in windows.security, and zeek HTTP shows only WebDAV file transfers. The only auth-adjacent events are 4648 explicit-credential logons by 'pbeesly' via PsExec, which is credential use, not MFA request generation.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: Certificate/private-key export to .pfx files via Get-PrivateKeys on scranton is consistent with stolen certificate abuse.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

findings.title: PowerShell process opened LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1FFFFF) on scranton
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z on scranton.dmevals.local, a PowerShell.exe process (PID 2976, user context SYSTEM) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1F3FFF, the access masks used to read LSASS memory for credential dumping. This occurred in the middle of a pbeesly-driven attack chain (Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-Exfil, Invoke-SeaDukeStage) on the same host, and the same PowerShell session had earlier run 'get-process'. A second LSASS open with 0x1F3FFF came from wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z, consistent with PowerShell remoting (Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA) issued from scranton.

findings.title: lsass.exe creates C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG on scranton (SAM credential log artifact)
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 748) created C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG at 03:19:09.994. A PASSWD.LOG written by lsass in the debug directory is a classic SAM/credential-dump artifact, appearing minutes after the attacker's LSASS handle acquisition and SAM hive access.

findings.title: PowerShell and wsmprovhost request full-access handles to lsass.exe on scranton/nashua
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe running as pbeesly requested a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with Access Mask 0x1F3FFF (includes 'Read from process memory', 'Write to process memory', 'Duplicate handle into or out of process'), and Sysmon recorded the same PowerShell process opening lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (pbeesly) also opened lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff. These are credential-capture accesses to LSASS memory, not normal system behaviour (the baseline LSASS opens are svchost.exe with 0x1000).

findings.title: Reflective in-memory API resolution (GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle) via PowerShell on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block (Event 4104, ScriptBlockId bc19aae2-d1f9-49b2-b718-192531ae928f) that reflectively resolves native APIs: it fetches Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods from System.dll, calls GetModuleHandle/GetProcAddress, defines a dynamic assembly named 'ReflectedDelegate' with a delegate type, and then decodes a base64 shellcode blob ([System.Convert]::FromBase64String("/EiD5PDozAAAA...")) for in-memory execution. This is the classic pattern for hooking/intercepting native credential APIs without touching disk. It is preceded by a hidden base64-encoded PowerShell launch (powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -e ...) and a steganographic loader reading C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png into IEX.

On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:14 and 00:35:25 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) connected to 192.168.0.4 over SMB (tcp/445 and tcp/139) and then issued 36 HTTP requests to port 80 using the Windows WebDAV redirector user agents 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' and 'DavClnt'. The requests were OPTIONS and PROPFIND to /webdav, /webdav/, /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z and /webdav/python.exe. The PROPFIND requests carried an AUTHORIZATION header (client_header_names includes AUTHORIZATION) and the server answered 401 Unauthorized before returning 207 Multi-Status, i.e. the host's credentials were coerced and accepted by the remote WebDAV listener. This is the classic T1187 forced-authentication chain (SMB/WebDAV UNC trigger -> NTLM credential capture) against an attacker-controlled listener at 192.168.0.4. All 36 WebDAV requests originate from 10.0.1.4 and target 192.168.0.4 only.
findings.title: WebDAV/SMB forced-authentication coercion from scranton (10.0.1.4) to 192.168.0.4

findings.summary: On 2020-05-02T03:21:29Z on scranton.dmevals.local, a PowerShell script block (ScriptBlockId bc19aae2-d1f9-49b2-b718-192531ae928f, PID 8784, user pbeesly, SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) was executed that resolves Win32 APIs via Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle, builds an in-memory delegate through DefineDynamicAssembly('ReflectedDelegate')/DefineDynamicModule('InMemoryModule'), and decodes a base64 blob beginning with a PE header ('/EiD5PDozAAAAEFRQVBSUVZ...'). This is a reflective shellcode/PE loader (obfuscated function names jzI/yT, variables yKR/cq/uJ) — the standard vehicle for in-memory credential-access tooling. It is corroborated by LSASS process-access events on the same host minutes earlier: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF (full access) at 03:05:16Z, and on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, WinRM, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29Z with a call trace through Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management. Full-access handles to LSASS from PowerShell/WinRM are consistent with credential dumping driven by the loaded payload.
findings.title: Obfuscated PowerShell reflective shellcode loader on scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly)

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly launched C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\accesschk.exe (parent process powershell.exe, integrity High), and one second later that process created the file C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB. The tooling was staged by the same PowerShell session that downloaded/extracted SysinternalsSuite and ran the Get-PrivateKeys certificate-theft function, so this is consistent with an adversary searching for credentials stored in files (T1552.001). The command line carried no arguments, so the exact target of the search is not visible in the telemetry.

findings.title: Rar.exe on nashua creates password-protected working.zip then sdelete64 wipes it

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script (readme.ps1 in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite) defining a Get-PrivateKeys function that enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and exports every certificate with a thumbprint to a randomly-named .pfx file under the user's Downloads folder, protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. This is direct private-key/certificate theft (T1552.004). It is part of a larger intrusion chain on the same host/user: a .scr payload executed from C:\ProgramData\victim, PowerShell download/extraction of SysinternalsSuite, accesschk.exe credential hunting, and an Invoke-Exfil function that 7-Zip-compresses the Downloads folder with password 'lolol'.

The resulting file coyn5igj.3io.pfx was written at 03:04:57. This is private-key/certificate theft beyond the anchored export description.

findings.title: PowerShell and PowerShell Remoting processes opened LSASS with full-access masks on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, user pbeesly's PowerShell activity on scranton.dmevals.local and nashua.dmevals.local opened handles to lsass.exe with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-class masks (0x1fffff, 0x1f3fff), the access pattern used to read credential material from LSASS memory. On scranton, PowerShell.exe (pid 2976) accessed lsass.exe (pid 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF and 0x1F3FFF at 03:05:16, with a CallTrace ending in UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D) - an unbacked/unknown module, not a normal Windows DLL path. That same pid 2976 was launched at 02:58:44 by control.exe with a hidden, execution-policy-bypass PowerShell command that decodes a steganographic payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX-executes it. On nashua, wsmprovhost.exe (PowerShell Remoting, pid 7720) accessed lsass.exe (pid 728) with 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29, its CallTrace running through PowerShell Management native images and multiple UNKNOWN modules. Windows Security object-access auditing (4656) independently records the same pbeesly/PowerShell and pbeesly/wsmprovhost LSASS accesses with AccessMask 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff. The only other high-mask LSASS access is MsMpEng.exe (Windows Defender), which is the benign baseline. This is credential access against LSASS by attacker-controlled PowerShell, not normal system behaviour.

findings.title: LSASS handle acquisition with full-access masks by attacker PowerShell (Credential Manager/DPAPI vault harvesting path)
findings.summary: The same LSASS accesses that support T1555 are the mechanism by which Windows Credential Manager secrets (DPAPI-protected vaults) are harvested: reading LSASS memory yields logon credentials and DPAPI material. On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly's powershell.exe requested a handle to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1fffff (Security 4656, AUDIT_SUCCESS), and on nashua.dmevals.local pbeesly's wsmprovhost.exe accessed lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff. No direct Credential Manager / vault / cmdkey command line or vault file access was observed (checks C217-C220 returned no hits), so the Credential Manager-specific artifact is inferred from the LSASS full-access reads rather than directly logged. The benign baseline for high-mask LSASS access is MsMpEng.exe (Windows Defender) and the CollectGuestLogs.exe Azure agent (0x1410/0x10).

findings.title: LSASS accessed with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by steganographic PowerShell loader (credential theft, not auth-process modification)
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, a hidden PowerShell process (PID 2976, entity_id {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) was spawned by control.exe running a steganographic loader that decodes C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX-executes the payload. That same process then opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS), the access mask used for LSASS credential dumping. This is credential theft from LSASS memory rather than modification of the authentication process itself; no authentication-process tampering (password filter, network provider, reversible encryption, MFA/hybrid identity) was observed.

On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z, the access mask used to read credential material from LSASS. The same PID 2976 was launched at 02:58:44 by user pbeesly with a hidden-window, execution-policy-bypass command that decodes a bitmap (C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png) into a byte array and pipes it to IEX — a steganographic payload loader. This is credential theft activity on the host.
findings.title: LSASS memory access with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by steganography-loaded PowerShell on scranton
PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On 2020-05-01T23:04:56 (host scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, powershell.exe PID 3876) a PowerShell script block defining function Get-PrivateKeys was executed. The function enumerates every certificate under cert:\LocalMachine recursively and, for each certificate with a Thumbprint, calls Export-PfxCertificate to write it to "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\$RandomFileName.pfx" protected by the hardcoded password "saribas". The script was loaded from Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1 (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b). Seconds later at 03:04:57.460Z Sysmon recorded the creation of the exported bundle C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe, and registry writes to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\MY\Certificates\48B5E43D09D080DF8863152FD22ED7C43443D499\Blob by powershell.exe on the same host. At 23:08:51 the same user ran function Invoke-BeachCleanup which deletes "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.pfx" (plus .bmp/.png and %APPDATA%\OfficeSupplies.7z), consistent with anti-forensic cleanup of the stolen certificate material. This is theft of authentication certificates/private keys (T1649).

findings.summary: On newyork.dmevals.local, 28 Kerberos service-ticket (4769) requests were logged, all with Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 (RC4-HMAC). Requests targeted machine/service accounts NASHUA$ (10), NEWYORK$ (11), SCRANTON$ (3) and WEC$ (1) with TicketOptions 0x40810000, issued to pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6. RC4 encryption on TGS requests is the hallmark of Kerberoasting, where an attacker requests service tickets to crack the service account password offline. findings.title: No password filter DLL registration or LSA notification package modification observed
findings.summary: Searches for password-filter/notification-package artifacts returned no hits: no 4657 registry changes to Notification Packages/Password/lsass keys, no 4688 process creation with Notification/PasswordFilter command lines, and no 4104 script blocks referencing Notification/PasswordFilter/lsass. findings.title: No reversible-encryption / AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption activity observed
findings.summary: No hits for reversible-encryption indicators: no 4739 (domain policy change) events, no 4688/1 process creations with Reversible/Set-ADUser/dsmod command lines, and no 4104/4103 script blocks referencing AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption or ReversibleEncryption. findings.title: No MFA modification activity observed
findings.summary: No 4739 domain-policy-change events and no 5136 directory-service-change events were found, and no process/script activity referencing Set-ADUser/Set-ADAccountControl or MFA-related changes. No evidence of multi-factor authentication being disabled or modified.

findings.title: No network provider DLL registration observed
findings.summary: No 4657 registry changes to NetworkProvider/Credential keys and no PowerShell script blocks referencing NetworkProvider/New-ItemProperty were found. No evidence of a malicious network provider DLL being registered to capture credentials.

findings.title: Network capture/ARP enumeration on scranton is Azure Guest Agent telemetry, not AiTM
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local (2020-05-02 ~03:19Z) SYSTEM ran 'netsh trace start capture=yes' writing an ETL to C:\windows\TEMP\<GUID>\...etl, 'netsh trace stop', 'ipconfig.exe /all' and 'arp.exe /a'. All of these are spawned by Azure guest-agent components (C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, CollectGuestLogs.exe), i.e. routine Azure VM diagnostic/telemetry collection, not adversary-in-the-middle positioning. No Responder/MITM tooling was found in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay; SMB traffic is normal DC-bound domain traffic
findings.summary: Sysmon DNS queries (event 22) are ordinary AD/Windows lookups (NEWYORK/NASHUA/SCRANTON, _ldap._tcp SRV records, wpad, Microsoft telemetry) with no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning pattern. Zeek SMB connections (port 445) all terminate in RSTO against the domain controller 10.0.0.4 and are tagged krb,smb,gssapi — normal authenticated domain traffic, not relayed authentication to an unauthorized host. The 23 Security 4697 service-install events are Windows default per-user services (svchost -k UnistackSvcGroup etc.) plus PSEXESVC from PsExec lateral movement, none of which is name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay.

findings.title: Synthetic placeholder MAC in Zeek capture is a lab artifact, not ARP cache poisoning
findings.summary: In the Zeek capture the responder L2 address 12:34:56:78:9a:bc appears on 559 of 613 connections — a well-known synthetic/placeholder MAC used in test datasets, not a real host claiming multiple IPs. The only ARP-related process activity is 'arp.exe /a' on scranton.dmevals.local, spawned by Azure guest-agent/telemetry components (WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe), i.e. routine diagnostic enumeration. No gratuitous-ARP or duplicate MAC-to-IP mapping indicative of ARP cache poisoning was observed.

findings.title: No DHCP activity present in any dataset — DHCP spoofing not observable
findings.summary: No DHCP-related telemetry exists in the collected data: windows.other contains no DHCP event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063), the Zeek capture has no dhcp log type (only conn/dns/http/ssl/kerberos/dce_rpc/smb_*), and Sysmon network-connect events show no traffic to DHCP ports 67/68. The only DHCP-adjacent process is the legitimate 'svchost.exe -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted -p -s Dhcp' service on scranton. With no DHCP client/server events captured, DHCP spoofing cannot be confirmed or refuted from this data.

The 4769 service-ticket requests observed (NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) all returned Failure Code 0x0 (success) and were issued by the KDC to legitimate principals; no service ticket was used without a corresponding KDC-issued request, and no anomalous service-account logon followed. No silver-ticket forging artifact was identified in the available telemetry.
findings.title: No silver-ticket (forged service ticket) evidence observed

findings.summary: No AS-REP roasting indicators were found: PowerShell script-block searches for AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth returned zero hits, and no 4768 pre-authentication-disabled ticket requests were observed in the security log. No forged web credential activity; LSASS access hits are benign system/PowerShell tooling
findings.summary: Across the 2020-05-02 02:55–03:28Z window on scranton/newyork/nashua/utica.dmevals.local there is no evidence of web-credential forging. The only LSASS process-access events with high access masks came from legitimate Windows binaries: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF on scranton at 03:05:16Z, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) opening lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF on nashua at 03:09:29Z (call trace through .NET/PowerShell Management native images). The remaining high-mask accesses (0x3000, 0x101001, 0x1000000) were svchost.exe/wininit.exe/csrss.exe on scranton. Logon process names for 4624/4648 were Kerberos (217), Advapi (76), User32 (2), NtLmSsp (1) — no anomalous authentication package. The 5857/5858 WMI events on newyork are routine RSOP_ExtensionStatus DeleteInstance operations by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (ClientProcessId 1588) with ResultCode 0x80041002. No cookie/SAML/token forging tooling was observed.

Routine certificate-store registry writes by legitimate Windows system processes
findings.summary: The bulk of certificate/crypto registry activity in windows.sysmon (1133 events matching Certificate/Crypto/Keys) and the windows.security 4657 hit on \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656 are attributable to normal OS components: lsass.exe updating AuthRoot certificate blobs, svchost.exe updating Windows Live ID Token Issuer and AuthRoot certificates, taskhostw.exe writing per-user ACRS PhysicalStores values, smss.exe writing the WOW6432Node SymbolicLinkValue, and the CertPropSvc instance of svchost.exe. These are standard certificate propagation/root-update operations, not adversary certificate theft.

findings.title: Kerberos TGT requests for pbeesly and SCRANTON$ are normal authentication
findings.summary: The 14 Kerberos AS-REQ (event 4768) events in windows.security are TGT requests for pbeesly (9) and the machine account SCRANTON$ (5), all with Status 0x0 (success), TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256) and TicketOptions 0x40810010, originating from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6. These are ordinary domain logon/TGT acquisitions and show no certificate-based (PKINIT) anomaly; they are not evidence of certificate theft or forging.

incidents.title: pbeesly multi-stage PowerShell credential/secret collection toolkit on scranton
incidents.rationale: F02 describes the surrounding pbeesly attack toolkit (Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-Exfil, Invoke-SeaDukeStage, Keystroke-Check, Invoke-ScreenCapture) on scranton; the credential-access component is general OS Credential Dumping (T1003).

incidents.title: LSASS memory access with full-access masks by attacker PowerShell/wsmprovhost on scranton and nashua
incidents.rationale: All six findings describe the same attacker action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, pbeesly/SYSTEM) and wsmprovhost.exe opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF on scranton and nashua on 2020-05-02. F32 and F34/F45 add the DPAPI/Credential Manager and steganographic-loader context but the observed action is the same LSASS handle acquisition, which best fits OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory (T1003.001).

incidents.title: lsass.exe creates PASSWD.LOG and opens SAM hive with KEY_ALL_ACCESS on scranton
incidents.rationale: F60 and F61 describe the same SAM credential-dump sequence on scranton: lsass.exe creating C:\Windows\debug\PASSWD.LOG at 03:19:09 followed by lsass.exe opening the SAM registry object with AccessMask 0xf003f (KEY_ALL_ACCESS) at 03:19:21-03:20:46, matching Security Account Manager (T1003.002).

incidents.title: Reflective in-memory API resolution and shellcode loader via PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: F08, F21 and F52 all describe the same PowerShell 4104 script block (ScriptBlockId bc19aae2-d1f9-49b2-b718-192531ae928f, user pbeesly) resolving GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle, building a ReflectedDelegate dynamic assembly and decoding base64 shellcode. F52 explicitly notes no SAML/token forging was observed, so the in-scope technique best matching the observed API-hooking/reflective-loading behavior is Credential API Hooking (T1056.004).

incidents.title: WebDAV/SMB forced-authentication coercion from scranton to 192.168.0.4
incidents.rationale: F19 describes scranton (10.0.1.4) connecting to 192.168.0.4 over SMB and issuing WebDAV PROPFIND/OPTIONS requests carrying an AUTHORIZATION header, the forced-authentication coercion pattern matching T1187.

incidents.title: accesschk.exe run by pbeesly creating a 'passwordsDB' file on scranton
incidents.rationale: F28 describes pbeesly launching accesschk.exe (parent powershell.exe) which created C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB, consistent with searching for credentials stored in files (T1552.001).

incidents.title: Sysinternals pspasswd.exe/pspasswd64.exe downloaded to Downloads on scranton
incidents.rationale: F58 describes PowerShell (pbeesly) writing pspasswd.exe and pspasswd64.exe into Downloads\SysinternalsSuite, credential/password-manipulation tooling staged for credential collection, consistent with T1552.001.

incidents.title: Rar.exe on nashua creates password-protected working.zip then sdelete64 wipes it
incidents.rationale: F62 describes pbeesly launching Rar.exe on nashua to create a password-protected archive working.zip (password fGzq5yKw) followed by sdelete64.exe wiping Rar.exe and both archive copies; password-protected staging plus anti-forensic cleanup is consistent with credential/data collection in files (T1552.001).

incidents.title: Invoke-Exfil compresses Downloads with password 'lolol' and exfiltrates to WebDAV with hardcoded creds
incidents.rationale: F63 describes pbeesly running Invoke-Exfil to compress the Downloads directory into password-protected OfficeSupplies.7z (password 'lolol') and copy it to \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd!, i.e. collection/exfiltration using embedded credentials, consistent with T1552.001.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exports LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on scranton
incidents.rationale: F27, F55 and F59 all describe the same action: pbeesly running Get-PrivateKeys from readme.ps1 to enumerate cert:\LocalMachine and export every certificate to random-named .pfx files (e.g. coyn5igj.3io.pfx) protected by hardcoded password 'saribas'. This is private-key/certificate theft, T1552.004.

incidents.title: Kerberos service-ticket requests for the krbtgt service with RC4 encryption
incidents.rationale: F47 describes three 4769 events requesting a krbtgt service ticket with RC4 encryption by pbeesly and SCRANTON$; unusual krbtgt service-ticket requests can accompany golden-ticket activity, best matching T1558.001, though no forged-ticket artifact was observed.

incidents.title: RC4-downgraded Kerberos service-ticket requests for machine accounts (Kerberoasting pattern)
incidents.rationale: F46 describes 28 Kerberos 4769 service-ticket requests with RC4-HMAC encryption for machine accounts NASHUA$, NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, WEC$ by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL, the Kerberoasting pattern matching T1558.003.

incidents.title: PsExec-delivered python.exe lateral movement and C2 on nashua
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same action: PsExec64.exe with explicit credentials launching C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua (parent PSEXESVC.exe) with outbound TCP to 192.168.0.4:8443 and WebDAV retrieval of python.exe. This is credential-based lateral movement/remote execution, not credential access; best ATT&CK fit is T1021 (Remote Services).
